explain.say: About half the world's drinking water comes from underground, and India pumps more groundwater than any other country. It lives not in underground lakes but in the pores of sand, gravel and cracked rock, called aquifers. On the board, a slice through the ground from the surface down.

explain.say: The top aquifer is unconfined: its upper surface is the water table, free to rise and fall. Below a clay layer, which barely lets water through, sits a confined aquifer, held under pressure. Drill into it and water can rise up the borehole by itself, sometimes gushing out: an artesian well. Which aquifer refills faster after rain?

explain.say: The unconfined one, since rain soaks straight in. Now switch on a pump. The water table dips into a funnel around the well, the cone of depression. See the curve: steep near the well, flattening out a hundred metres away, where the pumping barely shows. The dip at the well, here five metres, is called the drawdown.

explain.say: How much can the well give? For an unconfined aquifer, the Thiem equation uses the permeability and the water heights at two distances. With K of ten metres per day, twenty metres of water a hundred metres away and fifteen at the well, the well yields about eight hundred and forty six cubic metres a day.

explain.say: Pump too much and the cones spread and the water table falls year after year. In Mexico City and Jakarta, over-pumping has made the ground itself sink, in places by tens of centimetres a year, as clay layers compact: the same consolidation you met in soil mechanics. Wonderful! Challenge: why do wells near the sea sometimes turn salty?

faq.a: An aquifer is a layer of soil or rock, such as sand, gravel or fractured limestone, that holds water in its pores and lets it flow easily enough to supply wells.

faq.q: What is the difference between confined and unconfined aquifers?
faq.a: An unconfined aquifer has the water table as its upper surface and is recharged directly from above. A confined aquifer is sealed above by a low-permeability layer such as clay, so its water is under pressure.

faq.q: What is a cone of depression?
faq.a: It is the funnel-shaped lowering of the water table around a pumping well. It is steepest near the well and fades with distance.

faq.q: How do you calculate the yield of a well?
faq.a: For steady pumping from an unconfined aquifer, use the Thiem equation: Q equals pi K times (h2 squared minus h1 squared), over the natural log of r2 over r1. Our example gives about 846 cubic metres per day.

faq.q: Why does over-pumping groundwater make the ground sink?
faq.a: Lowering the water table reduces pore water pressure, so effective stress rises and clay layers consolidate. The ground surface subsides, as in Mexico City and Jakarta.

facts: Groundwater supplies roughly half of the world's drinking water.
India is the world's largest user of groundwater.
Parts of Jakarta have sunk by up to about 25 centimetres a year, largely due to groundwater extraction.

quiz.say: Using the Thiem equation with K of 5 metres per day, h2 of 20 metres, h1 of 18 metres and a log ratio of 6, what is the well yield?
quiz.show: Thiem: K = 5 m/day, h₂ = 20 m, h₁ = 18 m, ln(r₂/r₁) = 6. Yield Q = πK(h₂² − h₁²)/ln(r₂/r₁)?
quiz.why: π × 5 × (400 − 324) / 6 = π × 5 × 76 / 6 ≈ 199 cubic metres per day.

wrong.2: That forgets to divide by the log term, 6.
